content: Ulcerations and amputations are frequent complications observed in individuals with diabetes. These complications often arise as a result of peripheral neuropathy, peripheral arterial disease (PAD), or structural deformities of the foot. Early identification of feet that are at risk for these complications is critical in preventing severe outcomes. The risk factors contributing to the development of foot ulcerations and potential amputations include: Poor glycemic control, which exacerbates the progression of diabetes-related complications. Peripheral neuropathy, which diminishes protective sensation in the feet, increasing the likelihood of unnoticed injuries. Peripheral arterial disease (PAD), which impairs blood flow to the lower extremities, delaying wound healing. Preulcerative lesions, such as calluses or blisters, which can progress to open wounds if not addressed. A history of prior foot ulcers or amputations, which indicates a higher likelihood of recurrence. Smoking, which worsens vascular health and impairs healing processes. Coexisting conditions such as diabetic nephropathy or retinopathy, which reflect advanced systemic complications of diabetes and may indirectly increase the risk of foot-related issues.
